ch01.note: Iga, and its neighbour Kōga just across the passes in Ōmi, were the two districts of central Japan most closely tied to the shinobi — the spies and infiltrators for hire later romanticised as ninja. The whole world of the novel rests on this.

The nineteenth year of the Tenshō era: 1591. By this date Toyotomi Hideyoshi had all but completed the reunification of Japan begun by Oda Nobunaga. The novel keeps the old lunar calendar, on which the third month falls in spring.

A shaku is about 30.3 cm, so the staff runs to roughly 2.1 metres. The novel keeps the Japanese measures throughout — length (shaku, sun), distance (ri, chō, ken), yield (koku) — and glosses each at first use rather than converting it.

御斎峠, on the border of Iga and Ōmi and one of the seven passes leading out of the Iga basin. The name is usually read Otodo-tōge; Shiba gives it the softer reading Otogi (‘fairy tale’) that titles the chapter.

Tōyaku (当薬) is the dried herb Swertia japonica, ferociously bitter and a common folk remedy for the stomach. The old man's antique, dialect phrasing, and this rustic kindness, are what mark him to the woodcutter as a stranger from elsewhere.

The Tenshō Iga War. Nobunaga's son Nobukatsu invaded Iga in 1579 and was thrown back; in 1581 (Tenshō 9) Nobunaga invaded again and destroyed the province's warrior-league — the calamity that hangs over the whole novel. The event and its date are well attested. Shiba's figure of ‘more than twelve thousand’ Oda troops (given later in the chapter) is a modest one; modern estimates of the second invasion run as high as forty to sixty thousand.
A chō (also written 町) is about 109 metres.
Rappa (乱波) is an eastern-Japanese word for a shinobi: a spy, scout and saboteur for hire. Shiba uses rappa, shinobi and ninja for the same men.

Jizamurai, literally ‘samurai of the soil’: minor warriors who worked their own land and served no lord. In Iga they governed themselves through the sworn league the passage goes on to describe, and it was from their households that the ninja came.

In the sixth month of Tenshō 10 (June 1582) Nobunaga's own general Akechi Mitsuhide turned on him and killed him at the Honnō-ji, a temple in Kyoto. Nobunaga's ally Tokugawa Ieyasu, caught nearby at Sakai with only a handful of men, escaped home by exactly the secret route across Iga described here — the celebrated ‘divine lord's crossing of Iga.’

In 1571 Nobunaga stormed and burned Enryaku-ji, the great Tendai monastery on Mount Hiei above Kyoto, killing thousands. With his massacres of the militant Ikkō Pure-Land leagues at Ishiyama and Nagashima, it stands for his war on independent religious power — the hatred of the irrational Shiba makes of him in this passage.

The ichinomiya, or first shrine, of Iga province. The old chronicles record that when Nobunaga toured the conquered province late in 1581 and rested here, surviving Iga men led by Otowa-no-Kido fired on him with matchlocks and missed, killing only his guards. The episode is traditional rather than firmly documented.

A koku (about 180 litres of rice) was reckoned a year's food for one person, and a domain's worth was measured in koku. A stipend of a few thousand made these Sakai tea-merchants the equals of minor lords.

Sen no Rikyū, the supreme master of the tea ceremony, here under his lay name Sōeki; with Imai Sōkyū and Tsuda Sōgyū he was one of Hideyoshi's three tea masters. There is a quiet anachronism in the naming: Jirōzaemon speaks of Rikyū as a living stipendiary, but Hideyoshi had ordered him to commit suicide on the twenty-eighth of the second month of this very year, Tenshō 19 — a month before the scene, which is set late in the third.

ch01.anchor: the foot of the Great Buddha
ch01.note: The Great Buddha of the Hōkō-ji, the colossus Hideyoshi was raising in eastern Kyoto (begun 1588; the image finished about 1595, and soon lost to earthquake and fire). Even half-built, its precinct was a landmark and meeting-place in the capital.
A gatha (偈) is a Buddhist verse or hymn; the sunset gatha (日没偈) is one chanted at nightfall as part of the daily temple office.
